final.memo:
We have examined the company and have concluded that it does not meet our requirements for a durable, understandable business. While the firm possesses a portfolio of established entertainment franchises, the model requires constant creative reinvestment to maintain relevance rather than functioning as a self-maintaining royalty stream [D01, D06]. This continuous need to innovate, combined with significant competitive pressure for developer talent and consumer attention, makes the long-term earnings power difficult to predict [D06].

Furthermore, we are deeply concerned by the serious employment and workplace allegations currently facing the company [D01, D05]. These controversies present significant risks to management credibility and the stability of the creative pipeline, which are factors we cannot quantify and choose to avoid [D01, D05]. When we invest, we look for honest, able managers who act as owners of the business; the current uncertainties regarding culture and leadership suggest that such stability is currently lacking [D05].

Finally, we do not have sufficient visibility into the company's maintenance capital expenditures or debt structure to calculate owner earnings with any degree of confidence [D02, D04]. Given our $144.1 billion cash position, we have the luxury of patience and prefer to deploy capital into businesses that offer higher certainty and clear competitive advantages [D08]. We prefer to put this idea in our 'too hard' pile rather than risk Berkshire’s reputation and capital on an uncertain outcome [D01].
